questions.question: Engineers at a firm are quitting, citing 'no chance of promotion', even though HR data show promotion rates well above the industry average. Why does this matter, based on the slides' view of perception?

options.A: People act on what they perceive, not on objective reality
options.B: The HR data must be wrong, since staff know the truth best
options.C: Perceptions shape attitudes, but never actual behaviour
options.D: Turnover follows reality, so perceptions can safely be ignored

questions.note:
**Why A is correct:** Perception is how people organize and interpret impressions to give meaning to their environment; behaviour is based on perceptions of reality, not reality itself, so the world as perceived is what matters behaviourally. (Ch 2 slides: Perception)
**Why not B:** The slides don't say perceptions are more accurate than data; they say behaviour follows perception either way.
**Why not C:** Behaviour is based on perception, so perceptions drive what people do, including quitting.
**Why not D:** The reverse: the perceived world is the behaviourally important one.

questions.question: Two managers see the same employee leave at 4 p.m. One, who expects staff to slack off, sees laziness; the other, who knows the employee starts at 7 a.m., sees nothing wrong. Which factor in perception explains the difference?

options.A: The situation: the time of day and the work setting
options.B: The perceiver: their expectations and experience
options.C: The target: its background and proximity
options.D: The target: its novelty and motion

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** Factors in the perceiver (attitudes, motives, interests, experience and expectations) shape how the same target is interpreted; here the target and the situation are identical. (Ch 2 slides: Exhibit 2.1, Factors That Influence Perception)
**Why not A:** The time and setting are identical for both managers, so they can't explain the different readings.
**Why not C:** Nothing about the target's background or proximity differs between the two observers.
**Why not D:** The target is the same employee leaving at the same time for both managers.

questions.question: In an office of quiet, grey-suited staff, a new hire who wears a bright red jacket and laughs loudly is noticed by everyone on day one. Which factor influencing perception is mainly at work?

options.A: Characteristics of the perceivers, like their motives
options.B: Characteristics of the situation, like the time of day
options.C: Characteristics of the perceivers, like their interests
options.D: Characteristics of the target, like novelty and sound

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** Target characteristics such as novelty, motion, sounds, size, background, proximity and similarity affect what we notice; someone who stands out against the background gets noticed. (Ch 2 slides: Exhibit 2.1, Factors That Influence Perception)
**Why not A:** The observers vary, yet everyone notices; the trigger is what the target does and wears.
**Why not B:** The situation is an ordinary workday; the target's contrast with the background is what draws attention.
**Why not C:** Everyone notices regardless of their interests, which points to the target.

questions.question: A joke that gets big laughs at the staff barbecue falls flat when the same person tells it in a formal board meeting. Which factor influencing perception explains the different reactions?

options.A: The situation: the social and work setting
options.B: The perceiver: the listeners' fixed attitudes
options.C: The target: novelty and similarity of the joke
options.D: The target: the size and motion of the teller

questions.note:
**Why A is correct:** Situational factors such as time, work setting and social setting influence perception; the same target and behaviour are judged differently at a barbecue and in a boardroom. (Ch 2 slides: Exhibit 2.1, Factors That Influence Perception)
**Why not B:** Nothing suggests the listeners' attitudes changed; the context did.
**Why not C:** The joke and the teller are the same in both places; the setting changed.
**Why not D:** The teller is the same in both settings, so target characteristics don't explain the difference.

questions.question: A warehouse worker is curt with customers, co-workers and suppliers alike, whatever the situation. In attribution terms, what does this pattern suggest about the worker's curtness?

options.A: High consensus, pointing to an external cause
options.B: High distinctiveness, pointing to an external cause
options.C: Low consistency, pointing to an external cause
options.D: Low distinctiveness, pointing to an internal cause

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** Distinctiveness considers whether a person acts similarly across a variety of situations; behaving the same way everywhere is low distinctiveness, which points to an internal cause. (Ch 2 slides: Attribution Theory)
**Why not A:** Consensus concerns whether others act the same way in the same situation; the scenario says nothing about other workers.
**Why not B:** Distinctiveness would be high only if the curtness showed up in few situations; here it appears everywhere.
**Why not C:** Consistency concerns behaviour over time; the pattern described is across situations.

questions.question: A nurse who has been punctual every day for six years arrives late one morning. Using attribution theory, how is a supervisor likely to interpret this?

options.A: Low consensus, pointing to an internal cause
options.B: Low distinctiveness, pointing to an internal cause
options.C: High consistency, pointing to an internal cause
options.D: Low consistency, pointing to an external cause

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** Consistency considers whether a person has acted the same way over time; lateness that's rare for this nurse is low consistency, which points to an external cause. (Ch 2 slides: Attribution Theory)
**Why not A:** There's no information about whether others were late, and the key cue here is the nurse's own history.
**Why not B:** Distinctiveness concerns behaviour across different situations, which isn't what's described.
**Why not C:** Six years of punctuality makes the lateness inconsistent with past behaviour, not consistent.

questions.question: A manager reviewing an analyst's error-filled report learns three things: the analyst makes errors on all kinds of tasks, other analysts rarely make such errors, and this analyst has done so for months. What attribution is the manager likely to make?

options.A: External: low distinctiveness, high consensus, high consistency
options.B: Internal: low distinctiveness, low consensus, high consistency
options.C: External: high distinctiveness, high consensus, low consistency
options.D: Internal: high distinctiveness, low consensus, low consistency

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** In Exhibit 2.2, behaviour that happens in many situations (low distinctiveness), that others seldom show (low consensus) and that recurs over time (high consistency) is attributed to internal causes. (Ch 2 slides: Exhibit 2.2, Attribution Theory)
**Why not A:** Other analysts rarely make such errors, so consensus is low, not high.
**Why not C:** That pattern would point outward, but here the errors occur everywhere, few others make them, and they recur.
**Why not D:** Errors across all kinds of tasks for months mean low distinctiveness and high consistency.

questions.question: A delivery driver misses a deadline during a severe snowstorm, and the dispatcher concludes that the driver is careless. Which perceptual error is this?

options.A: Contrast effect
options.B: Self-serving attribution bias
options.C: Fundamental attribution error
options.D: Selective perception

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** The fundamental attribution error is underestimating external factors (the storm) and overestimating internal ones (carelessness) when judging others' behaviour. (Ch 2 slides: How Attributions Get Distorted)
**Why not A:** A contrast effect arises when a reaction to one person is shaped by others recently encountered.
**Why not B:** Self-serving bias concerns how people explain their own successes and failures, not someone else's.
**Why not D:** Selective perception is interpreting what you see through your interests, background and attitudes; the core error here is discounting the storm.

questions.question: At a performance-review workshop, most participants rate their own job performance as above average, and nearly all rate their sense of humour that way too. Which tendency from the slides does this illustrate?

options.A: Fundamental attribution error
options.B: Halo effect
options.C: Self-serving bias
options.D: Contrast effect

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** Self-serving bias is the tendency to credit successes to internal factors and blame failures on external ones; Exhibit 2.3 shows it in self-ratings (78% above average on performance, 96% on sense of humour, 84% on getting along). (Ch 2 slides: Self-Serving Bias, Exhibit 2.3)
**Why not A:** That error concerns judging other people's behaviour, not rating yourself.
**Why not B:** The halo effect is forming a general impression of someone from a single characteristic.
**Why not D:** Contrast effects come from comparing someone with people recently encountered, not from inflated self-ratings.

questions.question: A manager who opposes remote work notices every missed deadline by remote staff but overlooks the same lapses by people in the office. Which perceptual error is this?

options.A: Self-fulfilling prophecy
options.B: Contrast effect
options.C: Halo effect
options.D: Selective perception

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** Selective perception is interpreting what you see selectively, based on your interests, background, experience and attitudes; the manager's attitude toward remote work filters what gets noticed. (Ch 2 slides: Perceptual Errors)
**Why not A:** That's when people come to behave as others expect them to; nothing suggests the staff's behaviour changed.
**Why not B:** Contrast effects come from comparing someone with people recently encountered.
**Why not C:** The halo effect builds a general impression from one characteristic; here an attitude filters which lapses are noticed.

questions.question: Because a student has perfect attendance, an instructor assumes the student's essays must be equally strong and grades them generously. Which perceptual error is this?

options.A: Selective perception
options.B: Contrast effect
options.C: Halo effect
options.D: Stereotyping

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** The halo effect is drawing a general impression of a person on the basis of a single characteristic, here attendance. (Ch 2 slides: Perceptual Errors)
**Why not A:** The error isn't filtering what's seen through interests; it's generalizing from one positive trait.
**Why not B:** No comparison with recently encountered people is involved.
**Why not D:** Stereotyping judges someone by perceptions of a group they belong to; this judgment comes from one trait of the individual.

questions.question: A new accounts clerk seems remarkably fast to the team, mainly because the person who held the job before was extremely slow. Which perceptual error is shaping the team's view?

options.A: Stereotyping
options.B: Self-serving bias
options.C: Halo effect
options.D: Contrast effect

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** Contrast effects occur when our reaction to one person is influenced by other people we have recently encountered. (Ch 2 slides: Perceptual Errors)
**Why not A:** No group membership is involved; the judgment comes from comparison with the predecessor.
**Why not B:** Self-serving bias concerns how people explain their own successes and failures.
**Why not C:** The halo effect generalizes from one characteristic of the same person, not from a comparison with someone else.

questions.question: A team lead assumes that a new hire from a fine-arts program 'won't be good with numbers' and assigns the hire only writing tasks. Which perceptual error is this?

options.A: Fundamental attribution error
options.B: Halo effect
options.C: Contrast effect
options.D: Stereotyping

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** Stereotyping is judging someone on the basis of one's perception of the group to which that person belongs, here arts graduates. (Ch 2 slides: Perceptual Errors)
**Why not A:** That error concerns explaining someone's behaviour by internal rather than external causes; here no behaviour has occurred yet.
**Why not B:** The halo effect builds a general impression from one characteristic of the person, not from beliefs about a group.
**Why not C:** No comparison with recently encountered people is involved.

questions.question: A sales director is told that three new recruits are 'high-potential' (they were actually picked at random), treats them accordingly, and by year end they outperform their peers. Which concept does this illustrate?

options.A: Self-fulfilling prophecy
options.B: Selective perception
options.C: Halo effect
options.D: Contrast effect

questions.note:
**Why A is correct:** The self-fulfilling prophecy proposes that people behave in ways consistent with how others perceive them; the director's expectations shaped the recruits' performance. (Ch 2 slides: Why Do Perception and Judgment Matter?)
**Why not B:** Selective perception filters what an observer notices; here the recruits' actual results improved.
**Why not C:** The halo effect is a general impression formed from one characteristic; here expectations changed actual performance.
**Why not D:** Contrast effects come from comparisons with people recently encountered.

questions.question: A recruiter says they want to assess a candidate's personality, not their skills. According to the slides, what are they trying to assess?

options.A: The knowledge and abilities the person brings to the job
options.B: How they consistently react to and interact with others
options.C: The person's passing mood on the day of the interview
options.D: The person's beliefs about what is right and wrong

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** Personality is the sum total of ways an individual reacts to and interacts with others: stable patterns of behaviour and consistent internal states. (Ch 2 slides: What Is Personality?)
**Why not A:** Those are skills and abilities, which the recruiter has set aside.
**Why not C:** Moods are temporary feelings; personality refers to stable, enduring patterns.
**Why not D:** Beliefs about right and wrong relate to values and ethics, not personality.

questions.question: A firm can assess candidates' personalities through self-report surveys or through ratings from people who know them well. Which do the slides say tends to predict job success better?

options.A: Neither, since personality tests don't help with hiring
options.B: Observer ratings, which give an independent assessment
options.C: Self-report surveys, since people know themselves best
options.D: Self-report surveys, as they can't be faked by candidates

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** Self-report surveys have individuals rate themselves; observer ratings provide an independent assessment and tend to be more accurate predictors of success on the job. (Ch 2 slides: Measuring Personality)
**Why not A:** Research indicates personality tests are useful in hiring decisions.
**Why not C:** The slides say observer ratings, not self-reports, tend to be the more accurate predictors.
**Why not D:** The slides don't claim self-reports are fake-proof; they favour observer ratings for prediction.

questions.question: Two siblings raised in the same home differ sharply in how sociable they are, and both act more reserved at formal events than at parties. Which personality determinants do the slides list that could account for these patterns?

options.A: Environment alone, since upbringing shapes everything
options.B: Situations alone, since stable traits don't really exist
options.C: Heredity, environmental factors and situational conditions
options.D: Heredity alone, since personality is fixed at birth

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** The slides list three determinants of personality: heredity, environmental factors and situational conditions. (Ch 2 slides: Personality Determinants)
**Why not A:** Heredity and situational conditions are also listed as determinants.
**Why not B:** The slides define traits as enduring characteristics, alongside situational effects.
**Why not D:** The slides also list environmental factors and situational conditions as determinants.

questions.question: A team-development facilitator wants to use the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator with a project team that keeps clashing. Based on the slides, what's the most appropriate use?

options.A: Helping members better understand themselves and each other
options.B: Diagnosing which members have Dark Triad traits
options.C: Ranking members by how well each is likely to perform
options.D: Screening out members whose type predicts conflict

questions.note:
**Why A is correct:** Although widely criticized, the MBTI may help in training and development: helping employees understand themselves and each other, opening up communication and possibly reducing conflict. (Ch 2 slides: Myers-Briggs Type Indicator, For Managers)
**Why not B:** The MBTI taps four characteristics to sort people into 16 types; it doesn't measure the Dark Triad.
**Why not C:** The slides don't present the MBTI as a performance predictor; it classifies people into types.
**Why not D:** The slides suggest using MBTI results for development, not for screening people out.

questions.question: A long-term health study finds that employees who are responsible, organized, dependable and persistent not only perform better but also tend to live longer. Which Big Five trait fits?

options.A: Agreeableness
options.B: Conscientiousness
options.C: Emotional stability
options.D: Extraversion

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** In Exhibit 2.6, conscientiousness (effort, persistence, drive, discipline, organization) is linked to higher performance, enhanced leadership and greater longevity. (Ch 2 slides: Exhibit 2.6, How the Big Five Influence OB)
**Why not A:** Agreeableness is linked to being better liked and to lower deviant behaviour.
**Why not C:** Emotional stability is linked to job and life satisfaction and lower stress, not longevity.
**Why not D:** Extraversion is linked to interpersonal skills, leadership and satisfaction, not longevity.

questions.question: A warm, cooperative and trusting team member is well liked, goes along with group decisions and almost never breaks workplace rules. Which Big Five trait best explains this?

options.A: Agreeableness
options.B: Extraversion
options.C: Emotional stability
options.D: Conscientiousness

questions.note:
**Why A is correct:** Agreeable people are cooperative, warm and trusting; Exhibit 2.6 links the trait to being better liked, more compliant and conforming, and to lower deviant behaviour. (Ch 2 slides: Exhibit 2.6, How the Big Five Influence OB)
**Why not B:** Extraversion brings sociability and assertiveness, not compliance or lower deviance.
**Why not C:** Emotional stability is about calm and security, not warmth and compliance.
**Why not D:** Conscientiousness is about effort, organization and dependability rather than warmth and conformity.

questions.question: A training coordinator notices that the curious, creative and flexible employees get the most out of a new training program and adjust most easily to the changes it brings. Which Big Five trait does this reflect?

options.A: Extraversion
options.B: Openness to experience
options.C: Agreeableness
options.D: Conscientiousness

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** Openness (creative, flexible, curious) is linked in Exhibit 2.6 to increased learning, training performance, enhanced leadership and adaptability to change. (Ch 2 slides: Exhibit 2.6, How the Big Five Influence OB)
**Why not A:** Extraversion relates to sociability and assertiveness, not curiosity and creativity.
**Why not C:** Agreeableness relates to warmth and cooperation, not learning and adaptability.
**Why not D:** Conscientiousness relates to effort and organization; the learning and adaptability described point to openness.

questions.question: A company finds that its extraverted employees outperform others in team-based sales roles, but not in solitary data-entry jobs. What explains this, according to the slides?

options.A: Extraverts are simply more conscientious than other people
options.B: Solitary work lowers extraverts' emotional stability
options.C: Extraversion predicts performance mainly in highly social jobs
options.D: Extraversion predicts performance equally well in every job

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** Exhibit 2.6 links extraversion to higher performance in jobs requiring significant teamwork or frequent interpersonal interaction, drawing on better interpersonal skills and expressiveness. (Ch 2 slides: Exhibit 2.6, How the Big Five Influence OB)
**Why not A:** Conscientiousness is a separate Big Five trait; the gap tracks the social demands of the job.
**Why not B:** The slides don't say this; they tie extraversion's performance benefit to interpersonal jobs.
**Why not D:** The link is qualified: it applies to jobs with significant teamwork or frequent interaction.

questions.question: An employee is often distracted, disorganized and unreliable about deadlines. On which Big Five trait is this person likely to be low?

options.A: Conscientiousness
options.B: Emotional stability
options.C: Openness to experience
options.D: Agreeableness

questions.note:
**Why A is correct:** Exhibit 2.4 describes low conscientiousness as easily distracted, disorganized and unreliable; high conscientiousness is responsible, organized, dependable and persistent. (Ch 2 slides: Exhibit 2.4, Big Five Personality Traits)
**Why not B:** Low emotional stability shows up as hostility, anxiety, depression and insecurity.
**Why not C:** Low openness shows up as being unimaginative, inflexible, literal-minded and dull.
**Why not D:** Low agreeableness shows up as being cold, disagreeable and antagonistic.

questions.question: In supplier negotiations, a purchasing manager stays emotionally detached, uses whatever tactics work, believes the ends justify the means, and is rarely swayed by the other side. Which trait does this describe?

options.A: Psychopathy
options.B: Narcissism
options.C: High Machiavellianism
options.D: High self-monitoring

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** Machiavellianism is being pragmatic, keeping emotional distance and believing ends can justify means; high Machs manipulate more, win more, are persuaded less and persuade others more. (Ch 2 slides: The Dark Triad)
**Why not A:** Psychopathy is a lack of concern for others and no guilt or remorse when actions cause harm, linked to threats and bullying.
**Why not B:** Narcissism centres on arrogance, a grandiose sense of self-importance, a need for admiration and entitlement.
**Why not D:** High self-monitors adjust their behaviour to external cues; the core here is detachment and ends-justify-means pragmatism.

questions.question: A team lead constantly seeks admiration, feels entitled to the best assignments, and is sure they're the strongest leader in the department. What do the slides suggest about how their supervisors are likely to rate them?

options.A: About the same as everyone else on the team
options.B: As better leaders, but only when the team is in a crisis
options.C: As better leaders, since confidence signals real ability
options.D: As worse leaders than their peers, despite their own view

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** Narcissists tend to think they're better leaders than their colleagues, but their supervisors tend to rate them as worse. (Ch 2 slides: The Dark Triad)
**Why not A:** The slides report a clear gap: narcissists rate themselves better, while supervisors rate them worse.
**Why not B:** The slides make no such exception.
**Why not C:** The slides report the opposite: supervisors tend to rate narcissists as worse leaders.

questions.question: A department head shows no remorse when decisions harm staff and routinely uses threats and verbal intimidation to get results, while shrewdly accumulating power. Which Dark Triad trait does this best match?

options.A: Psychopathy
options.B: Narcissism
options.C: Machiavellianism
options.D: Low core self-evaluation

questions.note:
**Why A is correct:** Psychopathy is a lack of concern for others and no guilt or remorse when one's actions cause harm; it's linked to hard influence tactics like threats and to bullying, and its cunning can win power that isn't used toward healthy ends. (Ch 2 slides: The Dark Triad)
**Why not B:** Narcissism is about arrogance, entitlement and needing admiration rather than remorseless harm and intimidation.
**Why not C:** Machiavellianism is pragmatic manipulation and emotional distance; the lack of remorse and the bullying point to psychopathy.
**Why not D:** Low core self-evaluation means doubting your own capability and worth, which isn't described here.

questions.question: Two equally skilled engineers start on a hard project. One sees themself as capable, effective and in control; the other doubts their own competence. According to the slides, who is likely to perform better, and why?

options.A: Neither: skill alone decides how well each one performs
options.B: The first: they set bolder goals and persist longer
options.C: The first: they need less effort to reach their goals
options.D: The second: self-doubt makes people more careful

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** Core self-evaluation is the bottom-line conclusions people hold about their capabilities, competence and worth; people with positive core self-evaluations set more ambitious goals, are more committed to them and persist longer. (Ch 2 slides: Core Self-Evaluation)
**Why not A:** The slides say core self-evaluation itself affects performance through goals and persistence.
**Why not C:** The advantage comes from setting ambitious goals and persisting, not from needing less effort.
**Why not D:** The slides link positive, not negative, self-evaluations to better performance.

questions.question: Two colleagues have similar skills. One pays close attention to how others behave and readily adjusts to each situation. Based on the slides, how is this person's career likely to differ?

options.A: More promotions, more mobility and more central roles
options.B: Longer stays in one job, with less career mobility
options.C: Fewer promotions, since they seem inconsistent to bosses
options.D: Slower progress, since they conform too readily to others

questions.note:
**Why A is correct:** High self-monitors adjust behaviour to external, situational factors; they pay closer attention to others, conform more readily, are more mobile in their careers, receive more promotions and are more likely to hold central positions. (Ch 2 slides: Self-Monitoring)
**Why not B:** High self-monitors tend to be more mobile in their careers.
**Why not C:** The slides link high self-monitoring to more promotions, not fewer.
**Why not D:** Being capable of conforming is listed among high self-monitors' traits, alongside more promotions.

questions.question: An employee constantly spots opportunities, takes initiative and keeps pushing for change. In a rule-bound unit, some of these initiatives cause friction. What do the slides say about proactive personalities?

options.A: Their initiatives always improve the team's results
options.B: They tend to show lower job performance than their peers
options.C: Their actions can help or hurt, depending on context
options.D: They matter mainly in sales roles rather than other jobs

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** Proactive people identify opportunities, show initiative, take action and persevere until meaningful change occurs; they tend to have higher performance and career success, but their actions can be positive or negative depending on the organization and situation. (Ch 2 slides: Proactive Personality)
**Why not A:** The slides say proactive actions may be positive or negative depending on the context.
**Why not B:** Proactive personality is linked to higher job performance and career success.
**Why not D:** The slides don't limit proactive personality to sales; its effects depend on the organization and situation.

questions.question: In a nuclear plant's control room, rules are clear and consistent, constraints are tight and errors have severe consequences, so operators behave much the same whatever their personalities. Which theory explains this?

options.A: Affective events theory
options.B: Attribution theory
options.C: Self-fulfilling prophecy
options.D: Situation strength theory

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** Situation strength theory says the way personality translates into behaviour depends on the strength of the situation, analyzed in terms of clarity, consistency, constraints and consequences. (Ch 2 slides: Situation Strength Theory)
**Why not A:** AET explains how workplace events cause emotional reactions that shape attitudes and behaviour.
**Why not B:** Attribution theory explains how observers judge whether behaviour is internally or externally caused.
**Why not C:** That concept says people behave as others perceive them, which isn't described here.

questions.question: An employee has felt low and flat for two days without being able to point to any cause, and colleagues notice no telltale facial expression. According to the slides, what is this, and why?

options.A: An emotion: it is intense and aimed at a specific target
options.B: Neither: affect covers only short, intense feelings
options.C: A mood: it lingers, with no clear trigger or expression
options.D: An emotion: it is brief and shows clearly on the face

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** Moods are less intense than emotions and lack a contextual stimulus; they last hours or days, have general and unclear causes, and usually aren't shown by distinct expressions. (Ch 2 slides: Exhibit 2.7, Affect, Emotions, and Moods)
**Why not A:** Emotions are directed at someone or something, which this feeling isn't.
**Why not B:** Affect is the broad term covering both emotions and moods.
**Why not D:** Emotions are brief and usually come with distinct facial expressions; this feeling has lasted days with none.

questions.question: After a surprise announcement of layoffs, employees feel anxious and angry, and over the following weeks their job satisfaction and effort decline. Which model from the slides describes this chain?

options.A: Attribution theory
options.B: Affective events theory
options.C: Situation strength theory
options.D: The self-fulfilling prophecy

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** Affective events theory suggests that workplace events cause emotional reactions in employees, which then influence their workplace attitudes and behaviours. (Ch 2 slides: Affective Events Theory)
**Why not A:** Attribution theory explains how we judge the causes of others' behaviour, not how events trigger emotions that shape attitudes.
**Why not C:** That theory concerns how situational strength shapes the way personality shows up in behaviour.
**Why not D:** That concept is about people behaving as others expect them to.

questions.question: Planning a reorganization, a manager assumes staff will respond purely rationally and sets their feelings aside. What do the slides warn?

options.A: Only negative emotions need attention from managers
options.B: Rational analysis alone predicts staff behaviour best
options.C: Feelings are part of people, so they can't be set aside
options.D: Emotions matter only after a decision has been announced

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** The slides advise not ignoring co-workers' and employees' emotions or assessing behaviour as if it were completely rational; managers who understand emotions and moods explain and predict behaviour much better. (Ch 2 slides: OB at Work, For Managers)
**Why not A:** The slides also urge modelling positive emotions to foster decision making, creativity and motivation.
**Why not B:** The slides say understanding emotions significantly improves the ability to predict behaviour.
**Why not D:** The slides don't limit emotions' relevance to after decisions; they're part of how people respond throughout.

questions.question: After being passed over for a promotion they felt they deserved, an employee starts spreading rumours about a co-worker and blaming others for their own mistakes. Which category of employee deviance is this?

options.A: Property deviance
options.B: Political deviance
options.C: Production deviance
options.D: Personal aggression

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** Negative emotions can lead to employee deviance; the political category includes gossiping and blaming co-workers. (Ch 2 slides: Employee Deviance)
**Why not A:** Property deviance includes stealing and sabotage.
**Why not C:** Production deviance includes leaving early and intentionally working slowly.
**Why not D:** Personal aggression includes sexual harassment and verbal abuse.

questions.question: A flight attendant must appear calm and warm with passengers, even during a frightening stretch of turbulence. Which concept from the slides describes this part of the job?

options.A: Emotional labour
options.B: Affective events theory
options.C: Emotional intelligence
options.D: Self-monitoring

questions.note:
**Why A is correct:** Emotional labour is an employee's expression of organizationally desired emotions during interpersonal transactions at work. (Ch 2 slides: Emotional Labour)
**Why not B:** AET explains how workplace events trigger emotional reactions that shape attitudes and behaviour.
**Why not C:** EI is the ability to perceive, understand and regulate emotions; the requirement here is to display the emotions the employer wants.
**Why not D:** Self-monitoring is a personality trait about adjusting to external cues; a required display of emotions is emotional labour.

questions.question: An HR team learns that in the cascading model of emotional intelligence, each of the three abilities rests on a different individual factor. Which factor underlies the ability to regulate emotions?

options.A: Extraversion
options.B: Cognitive processing
options.C: Emotional stability
options.D: Conscientiousness

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** In Exhibit 2.8, conscientiousness supports perceiving emotions, cognitive processes support understanding them, and emotional stability supports regulating them. (Ch 2 slides: Exhibit 2.8, A Cascading Model of EI)
**Why not A:** Extraversion isn't part of the cascading model.
**Why not B:** Cognitive processes underlie understanding the meaning of emotions.
**Why not D:** Conscientiousness underlies the first step, perceiving emotions in self and others.

questions.question: In a tense meeting, a manager notices a colleague's frustration, realizes it stems from feeling ignored, and keeps their own irritation in check while responding. Which concept does this sequence illustrate?

options.A: Self-monitoring: adjusting to external situational cues
options.B: Emotional labour: displaying the required emotions
options.C: Affective events theory: events trigger reactions
options.D: Emotional intelligence: perceive, understand, regulate

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** EI is the ability to perceive emotions in self and others, understand their meaning, and regulate one's own emotions accordingly, in a cascading model. (Ch 2 slides: Emotional Intelligence)
**Why not A:** Self-monitoring is a trait about adapting behaviour to situations; perceiving, understanding and regulating emotions is EI.
**Why not B:** Emotional labour is about expressing organizationally desired emotions, not reading and understanding others' feelings.
**Why not C:** AET explains how events cause emotional reactions that shape attitudes, not a person's skill in handling emotions.

questions.question: A consultant urges a company to hire on the basis of emotional intelligence scores. Which point from the slides is part of the case against EI?

options.A: EI predicts criteria that matter, such as performance
options.B: EI has little intuitive appeal for most managers
options.C: Researchers disagree on how EI should be defined
options.D: EI is biologically based rather than simply learned

questions.note:
**Why C is correct:** The case against EI: researchers don't agree on definitions, EI can't be measured, and its validity is suspect. Intuitive appeal, predicting criteria that matter and being biologically based are arguments for it. (Ch 2 slides: The Case For and Against EI)
**Why not A:** That's an argument in favour of EI, not against it.
**Why not B:** Intuitive appeal is listed as part of the case for EI.
**Why not D:** Being biologically based is listed as part of the case for EI.

questions.question: A firm is deciding whether to invest in helping staff identify and manage their emotions. According to the slides, what does emotion management ability strongly predict?

options.A: Task performance and citizenship behaviours
options.B: Faster promotions and greater career mobility
options.C: Lower turnover and fewer sick days taken
options.D: Higher job satisfaction and lower stress

questions.note:
**Why A is correct:** Emotion regulation means identifying and modifying the emotions you feel, and emotion management ability is a strong predictor of task performance and organizational citizenship behaviours. (Ch 2 slides: Emotion Regulation)
**Why not B:** Those outcomes are linked in the slides to high self-monitoring, not emotion management.
**Why not C:** The slides don't list these; they name task performance and citizenship behaviours.
**Why not D:** Those outcomes are linked in Exhibit 2.6 to emotional stability.

questions.question: A manager is furious after learning that a key project was cancelled without consultation. Following the slides' advice on regulating intense emotions, what should the manager do?

options.A: Share the anger with the whole team at the next meeting
options.B: Vent directly to the executive who cancelled the project
options.C: Suppress the anger completely and say nothing at all
options.D: Vent only to a supportive listener who isn't involved

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** The slides advise recognizing the legitimacy of the emotion and venting only to a supportive listener who isn't involved in the event; acknowledging rather than suppressing emotional responses is one regulation strategy. (Ch 2 slides: OB at Work, For Managers)
**Why not A:** The advice is to vent to one supportive listener who isn't involved, not to the affected group.
**Why not B:** The advice is to vent only to a listener who isn't involved in the event.
**Why not C:** The slides list acknowledging rather than suppressing emotional responses as a strategy.

questions.question: A Canadian company wants to use a Big Five personality assessment in its offices in several countries. What do the slides say about the Big Five across cultures?

options.A: Personality can't be measured outside North America
options.B: Each culture needs an entirely different trait model
options.C: The five factors show up mainly in Western cultures
options.D: The five factors show up in nearly all cultures studied

questions.note:
**Why D is correct:** The slides note that the five Big Five factors appear in almost all cross-cultural studies. (Ch 2 slides: Global Differences)
**Why not A:** Nothing in the slides says this; the Big Five appears widely across cultures.
**Why not B:** The Big Five's appearance across almost all cultures argues against needing separate models.
**Why not C:** The slides say the factors appear in almost all cross-cultural studies, not mainly Western ones.

questions.question: Managers from two different cultures watch the same meeting and later recall different details and explain people's behaviour in different ways. What do the slides say about this?

options.A: Perception and attribution work the same in every culture
options.B: Culture affects what people notice, remember and attribute
options.C: Such differences come from personality, never from culture
options.D: Only emotions differ across cultures; perception doesn't

questions.note:
**Why B is correct:** Studies suggest cultural differences in perception affect what we focus on and remember, and most studies find cultural differences in the attributions people make. (Ch 2 slides: Global Differences)
**Why not A:** The slides cite evidence of cultural differences in both perception and attribution.
**Why not C:** The slides attribute these differences to culture, noting that even the Big Five appears across cultures.
**Why not D:** The slides describe cultural differences in perception and attribution as well as in emotions.
